Title: Building an inspiring classroom for architects
NewsSummary: The IED's workshop helped architects explore innovative teaching methods.
NewsContent:
Architecture is a profession that demands creativity and imagination. Designing spaces that stimulate people requires architects to manage a range of constraints related to the environment and the needs of residents. This means that asking questions and challenging assumptions is key to the learning process.

While the profession encourages invention and originality, teaching methods in classrooms continue to be old-fashioned. Instructors often choose to structure lessons in the form of long lectures where students are expected to be passive recipients of knowledge. 

As part of its efforts to address gaps in teaching practices, the Pakistan Council of Architects and Town Planners (PCATP) asked AKU's Institute for Educational Development, Pakistan, to conduct a week-long professional development programme for 24 faculty from 10 schools of architecture across Pakistan.

Explaining the need for the programme, Ms Zubeda Bana, Assistant Professor and the course coordinator from IED said: "Many university teachers do not hold formal teaching qualifications. The pressures of their work environment make them focus on completing courses on time instead of reflecting on learning outcomes, whether their teaching is actually benefiting students." 

"Through this professional development programme, we aim to guide teachers in how to continuously reflect on their teaching practices. This process enables them to evaluate whether their methods are working and empowers them to adopt different approaches in the class."

Sessions during the course required participants to reflect on the traits of a successful higher education teacher and the qualities associated with a good architect. A video highlighting the top ten qualities of architects was shown to the participants. Faculty were then given a self-inventory tool to assess whether the techniques they used were helping develop these traits in students and to explore ways in which they can enhance the understanding of key concepts in architecture.

Architect Seema Andaleeb, an assistant professor at NUST Islamabad and one of the course participants, said that she previously didn't know how to engage in self-reflection. 

"The courses helped me improve my teaching and to gain a deeper understanding of how to constantly reflect on my own practices to engage with my students in a more effective manner," she said.

The workshop also enabled teachers to practice their skills in creating an environment that makes students comfortable and encourages them to engage in a dialogue about what's being taught. Over the course of the week, each participant experimented with new techniques aimed at engaging students, reflected on their results and then incorporated feedback into subsequent sessions.  

By the end of the course, each participant had created personal plans outlining how they will modify and adjust their approach to teaching architecture.  

"Everyone remembers having a special teacher in school. Someone who made the classroom come to life and motivated them to give their best. Through these courses, we've given teachers the confidence to experiment. By encouraging teachers to focus on students rather than course content, we hope that this will help them make classes livelier and turn students into active participants in their learning," said Dr Munira Amirali, one of the course facilitators at IED.
